I looked for some sort of documentation/repo's on it all I found were disassemblers people made for it... lame well not really that's actually pretty cool just not what I want to use. 

But seeing this I think I have an idea in mind taking what other people have already done. Why not make a disassembler of my own to complete these challenges. Sounds pretty cool and all but I seem in over my head here but how hard can it be (*Future self: insert how hard it really is*). 

#### The Basics

Looking into the High Level Code, There is a bunch of functions here that seem to define different things within this language. 

We see a whole bunch of `interpret` calls. These seem to be interpreter instructions.
- `IMM`: The `interpret_imm` function calls `write_register` passing `arg2` which is the register name then `arg3` which is a 64-bit unsigned integer. So this sets the register values.
- `ADD`: Take the value of the two registers and store it in the first register.
- `STK`: If two arguments are passed push to the stack, are one argument is passed pop from the stack. Seems that you could both push and pop in the same call.
- `STM`: Set the first argument equal to the address of the second argument. Set Memory?
- `LDM`: Inverse of `STM`, set the first argument equal to the address of the fist argument. Load Memory?
- `CMP`: Checks if argument 1 is < > == != AND (arg1 != 0 && arg2 != 0) to argument 2 then it set the flags accordingly. Importantly this checks all these cases not just one.
- `JMP`: **Don't quite understand this one yet**, first argument is flags, second is a register.
- `SYS`: Syscall, see table below.

Registers:
- `a` / `0x8`: Syscall argument 1, GPR `arg1 + 0x100`
- `b` / `0x40`: Syscall argument 2, GPR `arg1 + 0x101`
- `c` / `0x10`: Syscall argument 3, Counter, GPR `arg1 + 0x102`
- `d` / `0x4`: GPR `arg1 + 0x103`
- `s` / `0x2`: Stack pointer, `arg1 + 0x104`
- `i` / `0x20`: Instruction pointer, `arg1 + 0x105`
- `f` / `0x1`: Flags `arg1 + 0x106`

Syscalls:
- `0x10`: Read memory, read the given memory via a register.
    - `a` = `fd`
    - `b` = location of `buf`
    - `c` = count
- `0x20`: Write the given memory, via the register location.
    - `a` = `fd`
    - `b` = location of `buf`
    - `c` = count
- `0x8`: Sleep
- `0x2`: Open
- `0x4`: Exit

With a somewhat basic understanding, ~~we can start to work on our disassembler~~... this was ditched for now. 

We can create some custom types with BinaryNinja to allow us to more easily understand what is happening when looking at the C disassembly of the program. These allow us to break down what we are looking at by changing the types pulled into each function. We define the following down below: `vm_reg` to differentiate between the registers, `vm_state` to block out the memory portions specifically where the registers sit, `vm_sys` to give names to each of the syscalls.

```c
enum vm_reg : uint8_t
{
    REG_F = 0x1,
    REG_S = 0x2,
    REG_D = 0x4,
    REG_A = 0x8,
    REG_C = 0x10,
    REG_I = 0x20,
    REG_B = 0x40
};

struct vm_state
{
    uint8_t _unknown[0x100];
    uint8_t a;
    uint8_t b;
    uint8_t c;
    uint8_t d;
    uint8_t s;
    uint8_t i;
    uint8_t f;
};

enum vm_sys : uint8_t
{
    SYS_READ = 0x10,
    SYS_WRITE = 0x20,
    SYS_SLEEP = 0x8,
    SYS_OPEN = 0x2,
    SYS_EXIT = 0x4
};
```

### Solving the Challenge

Once we change the types of the functions from what we understood above we can get a clearer picture as to what is happening.

![700](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261005155305.png)

We see that the first 4 lines read a value from `0` aka `STDIN` to `0x3f` via the read syscall. From here we then see `B` which previously held our memory location pointed at changed to `0x5f`. `C` is set to one and if we look at its usage throughout the program it is used to increment the value of `B`. Now we see `A` set to some hex value to we set the value of the memory location of `B` to `A`. This is done for 6 characters, `\x76\xa3\xea\x8b\x75\x8d`. 

After all those characters are pushed/moved onto the memory location at `0x5f` they are compared to the memory which was read from `STDIN` at `0x3f`.

![700](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261005155814.png)

If `memcmp` returns `0` it is then compared to `0` so it would result in a true or `1` value.

![700](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261005160404.png)

I added an `enum` to write out the characters as there values due to all the `SYS_WRITE` calls. If then `memcmp` comparison turns out to be false then we write `INCORRECT` out to the terminal with the start of that seen above. If the `memcmp` results in `true`, then we write out `CORRECT`.

![700](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261005160723.png)

Then following that we see the flag get opened and read.

![700](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261005160908.png)

If we run the following command in theory we should receive the flag.

```bash
echo -en '\x76\xa3\xea\x8b\x75\x8d' | /challenge/trust-the-yancode-easy
```

![](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261005160928.png)

![700](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261005161010.png)

## Know the Yancode (Easy)

### What is happening here?

After setting all the tables to the correct values, we can see that there is a whole bunch of checks on the `f`/flags register seeing if a previous compare was equal to each other if so don't set the incorrect variable else set the incorrect variable to then not give the flag. This program essentially does the exact same thing as the previous one except it uses a few new instructions to us. `IMM` and `LDM` are both used to compare the user input to the key. 

![700](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261005171040.png)

In the last couple of lines we see the value of register B get set to `5f` where the key lives and register A get set to `3f` where the user input lives. Each character is compared individually. We see the key here of `\xe2\xaf\x22\x60\x1c\x9b`.

## Master the Yancode (Easy)

### Solving the Challenge

This one is similar to the last but the difference is that the values are populated into memory then they have a value added to them.

![](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261005180432.png)

I highlighted the new additions above. 

The original six hex values are: 

`7c 3f fa f3 3d c8`

The values added onto them are:

`8a 7f 3f 7b be 1f`.

So now we will add these values together and grab the values to give to get the flag. I made a little script for this.

`add_master.py`

```python
a = [0x7c, 0x3f, 0xfa, 0xf3, 0x3d, 0xc8]
b = [0x8a, 0x7f, 0x3f, 0x7b, 0xbe, 0x1f]

for i in range(6):
    a[i] += b[i]
    
print([hex(x & 0xff) for x in a])
```

We get the following output.

`['0x6', '0xbe', '0x39', '0x6e', '0xfb', '0xe7']`

We reformat this to be the input into the program.

`\x6\xbe\x39\x6e\xfb\xe7`

Then we can run the program and grab the flag.


## Transcend the Yancode (Easy)

I won't explain analysis steps for this, but the original value is `46 12 db ad 7c 6e 93 47 8f`. The final input is modified by this key `a3 45 95 90 2b a1 99 9f ce`. If we subtract the modification from the original key value we can submit the key just like the previous challenge. The only difference is this `cmp`'s each value individually instead of the `memcmp`.

`sub_transcend_easy.py`

```python
a = bytearray.fromhex("46 12 db ad 7c 6e 93 47 8f")
b = bytearray.fromhex("a3 45 95 90 2b a1 99 9f ce") 

for i in range(len(a)):
    a[i] = (a[i] - b[i]) & 0xff

for x in a:
    print(f"\\x{x:x}", end='')
```

We modify our script ever so slightly with some quality of life changes. Now we can input our new input into echo and call it a day.

```bash
echo -ne '\xa3\xcd\x46\x1d\x51\xcd\xfa\xa8\xc1' | /challenge/transcend-the-yancode-easy
```

![700](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261005191143.png)

## Transcend the Yancode (Hard)

I won't explain analysis steps for this, but the original value is `4c 5b 15 a5 b4 14 f5 38 74 32 ee 5e`. The final input is modified by this key `a7 c9 5c a4 a0 de 05 73 26 6b f4 8d`. If we add the modification to the original key value we can submit the key just like the master easy challenge. The only difference is this `cmp`'s each value individually instead of the `memcmp`.

```python
a = bytearray.fromhex("4c 5b 15 a5 b4 14 f5 38 74 32 ee 5e")
b = bytearray.fromhex("a7 c9 5c a4 a0 de 05 73 26 6b f4 8d") 

for i in range(len(a)):
```

## The Yanalyzer (Easy)

### The Interpreter Loop

These are starting to become quite tedious...

#TODO ask simon: Would there be an easier solution to this than loading the types each time? I assume it is meant to be annoying as we have different values for the enum every.. single.. time :).

So this is interesting now we see an interpreter loop where instructions are now interpreted instead of a execute program function. 

![](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261005193935.png)

Looking into the program the offsets changed from `0x100` to `0x400` like the register definitions thus we need to update the `vm_state` struct. The names of the `code` and `memory_stack` are complete guesses based on the variable names at this point but it will help us with a definition in main. We change the type of the variable at `2356` to `vm_state` and the `vm_mem` to the type `uint8_t const vm_mem[0x100]` and now we have a bit of a cleaner picture.

```c
struct vm_state
{
    uint8_t code[0x300];
    uint8_t memory_stack[0x100];
    uint8_t a;
    uint8_t b;
    uint8_t c;
    uint8_t d;
    uint8_t s;
    uint8_t i;
    uint8_t f;
};
```

Once we change the type of the `interpreter_loop` function to include our `vm_state` type we now have a cleaner picture as to what is happening.

![](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261005195628.png)

We increment `i` the instruction pointer, take `i` multiply it be `3` and then add on the `vm_state`. This is interesting, I wonder if each instruction has a length of `3`. Now each instruction has a value associated with it. This is where our disassembler may be nice.

```
2: interpret_imm
40: interpret_add
1: interpret_stk
< 0 (80 found this through looking at the bytecode): interpret_stm
8: interpret_ldm
10: interpret_cmp
4: interpret_jmp
```

Upon further reading into the disassembly our assumption is correct each instruction has a fixed length of 3. Woot woot. Now we can create a new type for an instruction object. I named this `vm_instruction` as each object is made up of a `inst_arg2, inst_arg1, inst_opcode`.

```c
struct vm_instruction
{
    int8_t inst_arg2;
    int8_t inst_arg1;
    int8_t inst_opcode;
};
```

We then change the `vm_state` object to now include our new struct.

```c
struct vm_state
{
    struct vm_instruction code[0x100];
    uint8_t memory_stack[0x100];
    uint8_t a;
    uint8_t b;
    uint8_t c;
    uint8_t d;
    uint8_t s;
    uint8_t i;
    uint8_t f;
};
```

Once we add our new type definitions we can see how each opcode is used and read correlating to our instruction interpreting loop from which we got the above values.

![](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261005214204.png)

There is a few other things that need to be changed as well....

Syscall numbers are different... of course. On top of this there is a new syscall we now have `read_memory` and `read_code`. It will be interesting to see how these are used. On top of this every function takes two arguments now but they are pulled from the code instead of the function calls themselves. The functions in the pseudo-code get passed the `vm_instruction` in their second argument. 

```c
enum vm_reg : uint8_t
{
    REG_C = 0x1,
    REG_D = 0x2,
    REG_B = 0x4,
    REG_A = 0x8,
    REG_F = 0x10,
    REG_S = 0x20,
    REG_I = 0x40
};

enum vm_sys : uint8_t
{
    SYS_READ_MEMORY = 0x1,
    SYS_READ_CODE = 0x2,
    SYS_WRITE = 0x4,
    SYS_SLEEP = 0x20,
    SYS_OPEN = 0x8,
    SYS_EXIT = 0x10
};
```

Phew.. ok looking around we have finally torn apart most of this interpreter.. I left some details out but this is the gist of it.

Looking around we can pull out the bytecode for the virtual machine.

```

```

### The Disassembler Process

With the raw code we can now put it into a python file and begin our disassembler.

```python
code = bytearray.fromhex("")

REG = {1: 'c', 2: 'd', 4: 'b', 8: 'a', 0x10: 'f', 0x20: 's', 0x40: 'i'}
SYS = {1: 'read_memory', 2: 'read_code', 4: 'write', 0x20: 'sleep', 8: 'open', 0x10: 'exit'}
OPS = [(2, 'imm'), (0x40, 'add'), (1, 'stk'), (0x80, 'stm'), (8, 'ldm'), (0x10, 'cmp'), (4, 'jmp'), (0x20, 'sys')] # These have to be in order from how they are in the interpreter due to the ANDing funkiness
CON = {8: '<', 4: '>', 1: '==', 2: '!=', 0x10: '== 0'}
reg = lambda x: REG.get(x, 'NONE' if x == 0 else f'?{x:#x}') # NONE is needed for the stk command

INST_LEN = 3 # In case it gets changed later which I totally expect to happen

for n in range(len(code) // INST_LEN):
    current_rip = n * INST_LEN
    next_rip = current_rip + INST_LEN
    inst_arg2, inst_arg1, inst_opcode = code[current_rip:next_rip]
    
    instructions = []
    
    # We need to loop through all the OPCODE values ANDING against the current instruction OPCODE
    for bit, name in OPS:
        if bit & inst_opcode:
            if name == 'imm':
                # Add character interpretation (Not set on this kinda annoying when not needed)
                ascii_char = f"\t'{chr(inst_arg2)}'" if 0x20<=inst_arg2<0x7f else ''
                instructions.append(f"imm {reg(inst_arg1)} = {inst_arg2:#04x}{ascii_char}")
            elif name == 'add':
                instructions.append(f"add {reg(inst_arg1)} += {reg(inst_arg2)}")
            elif name == 'stk':
                instructions.append(f"stk push {reg(inst_arg2)} / pop {reg(inst_arg1)}")
            elif name == 'stm':
                instructions.append(f"stm *{reg(inst_arg1)} = {reg(inst_arg2)}")
            elif name == 'ldm':
                instructions.append(f"ldm {reg(inst_arg1)} = *{reg(inst_arg2)}")
            elif name == 'cmp':
                instructions.append(f"cmp {reg(inst_arg1)} {reg(inst_arg2)}")
            elif name == 'jmp':
                c = ' | '.join(v for k, v in CON.items() if inst_arg1 & k) or f'{inst_arg1:#x}'
                instructions.append(f"jmp if {c} dest: {reg(inst_arg2)}")
            elif name == 'sys':
                s = ' | '.join(v for k, v in SYS.items() if inst_arg1 & k) or f'{inst_arg1:#x}'
                instructions.append(f"sys {s} -> {reg(inst_arg2)}")
                
    print(f"{n:02x}: {inst_arg2:02x} {inst_arg1:02x} {inst_opcode:02x}   " + ('; '.join(instructions) or '???'))
```

### Solving the Challenge

Breaking down what we have we go to our entry point where it looks like our key is defined.

![700](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261006094749.png)

It looks like the key goes from `0x62` to `0x6c`, following execution is where we get our input buffer from `STDIN`.

Once that happens we are then put into a loop starting at `0x17`.

![700](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261006095134.png)

This loop starts by populating `a-d`. The return address is pushed and then the function is `called` it loops through the memory from both `64-6c` and `30-39` starting at the top of the index and subtracting 1 on the pointer each loop iteration. Checking if each character matches one another and then if the counter has hit zero yet. 

![700](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261006100832.png)

Assuming we can return if our input is correct, then `c`  is compared to `d` these should be the same as `c` was just moved into `d` with the value zero after the loop was done unless broken by `0x0e` in which case `d` would be the loop iteration number which wouldn't be 0. If they are the same we can see that we jump to `0x4b` which starts the `CORRECT` string and flag reading sequence.

![](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261006100847.png)

Knowing our key starts its comparison at `0x64` and it is `9` bytes long we grab this value from the code and should be able to grab our key.

`11 72 90 61 ec 3d c2 4b 7e`

We can then replicate this sequence in `ipython3` to get the flag.

![](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261006101315.png)

![](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261006101241.png)

## The Yannalyzer (Hard)

The register values changed...

Lucky for us we have this constants section so we can just change them in our `r2` clone.

```python
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Per-level encoding (these get randomized, so they live up here)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
INST_LEN = 3
ARG2_IDX, ARG1_IDX, OP_IDX = 0, 1, 2

REG = {1: 'b', 2: 'a', 4: 'f', 8: 's', 0x10: 'd', 0x20: 'i', 0x40: 'c'}
SYS = {1: 'read_memory', 2: 'read_code', 4: 'write', 0x8: 'sleep', 0x10: 'open', 0x20: 'exit'}
# Must be in the same order the interpreter tests the bits
OPS = [(8, 'imm'), (0x40, 'add'), (0x80, 'stk'), (0x10, 'stm'), (2, 'ldm'),
       (0x1, 'cmp'), (4, 'jmp'), (0x20, 'sys')]
CON = {4: '<', 1: '>', 2: '==', 0x10: '!=', 0x8: '==0'}

# Which registers each syscall reads, for the argument comment
SYS_ARGS = {
    'read_memory': ('fd', 'a'), 'read_code': ('fd', 'a'),
    'write': ('fd', 'a'), 'open': ('path', 'a'),
    'sleep': ('secs', 'a'), 'exit': ('code', 'a'),
}
```

Now looking over the code we can see that we once again take a user input that is `0x1b` bytes long. On top of this values to each point that we read are added onto by a value like we first saw with Master The Yancode (Hard). 

![](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261006120207.png)

This goes on and on but they value added to our key is: 
`f9 c5 21 23 26 85 1a 05 75 66 5b 85 98 14 71 25 1d bd 23 d8 31`.

Now we must get the final key value then we can subtract the two to get the initial key input. Lucky for us the new version of our script can pull this already.
![](Attachments/Pasted%20image%2020261006120419.png)

`41 5d 50 99 79 3b 5d 55 f4 eb c6 49 8a a5 0d 6a 50 ce b9 31 0e`

Now we can use our `a`/`b` `sub` script to get our key value.

`sub_yangler_easy.py`

```python
a = bytearray.fromhex("41 5d 50 99 79 3b 5d 55 f4 eb c6 49 8a a5 0d 6a 50 ce b9 31 0e")
b = bytearray.fromhex("f9 c5 21 23 26 85 1a 05 75 66 5b 85 98 14 71 25 1d bd 23 d8 31")

for i in range(len(a)):
    a[i] = (a[i] - b[i]) & 0xff

for x in a:
    print(f"\\x{x:x}", end='')
```

```bash
echo -ne '\x48\x98\x2f\x76\x53\xb6\x43\x50\x7f\x85\x6b\xc4\xf2\x91\x9c\x45\x33\x11\x96\x59\xdd' | /challenge/the-yangler-easy
```

The raw code is here:


```python
ARG2_IDX, ARG1_IDX, OP_IDX = 0, 1, 2

REG = {1: 'c', 2: 'b', 4: 'a', 8: 's', 0x10: 'f', 0x20: 'i', 0x40: 'd'}
SYS = {0x20: 'read_memory', 1: 'read_code', 0x1: 'write', 0x4: 'sleep', 0x2: 'open', 0x8: 'exit'}
# Must be in the same order the interpreter tests the bits
OPS = [(0x20, 'imm'), (0x2, 'add'), (0x80, 'stk'), (0x1, 'stm'), (0x8, 'ldm'),
       (0x40, 'cmp'), (0x10, 'jmp'), (0x4, 'sys')]
CON = {0x10: '<', 2: '>', 0x4: '==', 0x8: '!=', 0x1: '==0'}
```

Once we set all of this up we run the program and we obtain the final comparison key and initial key.

Final Key:

`48 3e 97 48 65 43 06 3b ea 8f fd 4b 07 e8 14 fd b1 5e 1d 87 a2`

Initial Key Addition:

`bc b1 07 8f 7d 36 d3 89 d2 dd 5b 37 10 f7 17 58 8f eb 7d 56 1f`

`sub_yangler_hard.py`

```python
a = bytearray.fromhex("48 3e 97 48 65 43 06 3b ea 8f fd 4b 07 e8 14 fd b1 5e 1d 87 a2")
b = bytearray.fromhex("bc b1 07 8f 7d 36 d3 89 d2 dd 5b 37 10 f7 17 58 8f eb 7d 56 1f")

for i in range(len(a)):
    a[i] = (a[i] - b[i]) & 0xff

for x in a:
    print(f"\\x{x:x}", end='')
```

See this is where I have bent the line with Claude. After hours and hours of doing this I am quite sick of spending 10 minutes grabbing and updating all the offsets. As such I had Claude write a script to analyze the executable with `binutils` and pull out the constants so we can get to the actual analysis. Having done this manually a plethora of times I think it is fair to automate this process. Well this was all cool, and they do work... we are writing our own Yancode now so there is no code to tear apart. Luckily we have plenty of examples on how to read `/flag` in Yancode so our pseudo code will look something like this (This was taken from `the-yanalyzer-easy` disassembly).

```
imm d, 0x2f
imm c, 0x80
stm [c], d
imm d, 0x66
imm c, 0x81
stm [c], d
imm d, 0x6c
imm c, 0x82
stm [c], d
imm d, 0x61
imm c, 0x83
stm [c], d
imm d, 0x67
imm c, 0x84
stm [c], d
imm d, 0x00
imm c, 0x85
stm [c], d
imm a, 0x80
imm b, 0x00
sys OPEN, d
imm b, 0x00
add b, s
imm c, 0xff
imm a, 0x00
add a, d
sys READ_MEMORY, d
imm b, 0x00
add b, s
imm c, 0x00
add c, d
imm a, 0x01
sys WRITE, d
imm a, 0x00
sys EXIT
```
